<explanation>
Below is a tailored guide on how to draw a comprehensive system-design diagram for **json-server**, an open-source CLI tool that spins up a full fake REST API backed by a JSON file. This will help your team understand its internal components, their interactions, and extension points.

1. Identify the Project Type and Purpose
   • Type: Open-source CLI tool / HTTP server library  
   • Purpose: Read one or more JSON/JSON5 files (e.g., `db.json`), spin up an Express-based HTTP server exposing CRUD REST endpoints, serve static files, and watch for file changes to update the in-memory database.

2. Analyze the File Structure
   Top-level directories and their roles:
     – src/  
       • bin.ts  → CLI entrypoint: parse args, locate DB files, initialize the app  
       • app.ts  → Primary Express app factory  
       • service.ts → Implements in-memory DB operations (CRUD, filters, pagination, embed)  
       • observer.ts → File-watcher that reloads DB on disk changes  
       • *.test.ts → Unit tests for core modules  
     – fixtures/  
       • db.json(.json5) → Example data inputs  
     – public/ & views/  
       • public/test.html, views/index.html → Static UI or demo pages served by Express  
     – Config & metadata  
       • package.json, tsconfig.json, ESLint, Husky, Prettier configs  
     – .github/workflows/ → CI pipelines (build, test, npm-publish)

3. Extract Insights from README
   – The CLI (`npx json-server db.json`) boots the tool, serving REST routes based on top-level keys in the JSON.  
   – It supports query params for filtering, sorting, pagination, embedding, and conditional operations.  
   – It serves any `./public` directory contents as static assets.  
   – It uses the Fair Source License; sponsorship hooks are purely for funding.

4. Main Components and Their Relationships
   Your diagram should include these core boxes and flows:

   [CLI Layer]
     • bin.ts  
     – Parses CLI args, paths to DB file(s), port, other flags  
     – → Instantiates AppFactory (app.ts) with config

   [Application Layer]
     • app.ts (Express app)  
       – Middleware chain: JSON parser, query-parser, logger, CORS, static-file serving  
       – Routes registration: CRUD endpoints per resource (via service.ts)  
       – Error handlers

   [Service / Data Layer]
     • service.ts  
       – In-memory JS object (`db`) holding data loaded from disk  
       – Implements CRUD operations, filtering logic (`?views_gt=9000`), pagination, sorting, embedding  
       – Exposes methods that Express routes call for each HTTP verb

   [Persistence / File System]
     • observer.ts  
       – Watches DB file(s) for change events (fs.watch)  
       – On change, re-parse JSON/JSON5 and update in-memory `db`  
       • Optionally writes back to disk when creating/updating/deleting via CLI flags  

   [Static Assets]
     • public/, views/  
       – Served by Express when `-s/--static` is provided or default `public` folder exists  
       – Optional demo UI (`test.html`, `index.html`)

   [External Dependencies]
     • Express.js (HTTP server)  
     • JSON5 parser  
     • chokidar or fs.watch (file watching)  
     • Commander or yargs (for CLI parsing)

5. Architectural Patterns & Design Principles
   – Modular separation: CLI bootstrap, HTTP app factory, service (business logic), observer (side-effect management)  
   – In-memory DB with optional persistence: allows fast CRUD and hot reload  
   – Middleware pipeline for cross-cutting concerns (logging, static, error handling)  
   – Extensibility points: you can mount additional static folders, extend routes via custom middleware, swap out storage layer

6. Tailoring the Diagram for an Open-Source CLI Tool
   – Highlight the **CLI** box at the top, showing user input → config  
   – Emphasize the **Express App** box as central hub  
   – Draw arrows:  
     • CLI → AppFactory  
     • AppFactory → Service (for data ops)  
     • Observer ↔ Service (watch & reload)  
     • AppFactory → Static Asset folders  
     • AppFactory → HTTP requests (REST clients)  
   – Show external storage (the JSON file on disk) and static file directory as rectangular boxes on the side  

7. Diagramming Guidelines
   – Use **clear labels** for each component (e.g., “bin.ts (CLI)”, “app.ts (Express Server)”)  
   – Use **directional arrows** to show control flow (CLI → App) and data flow (HTTP Request → Service → JSON file)  
   – Apply **color coding** or shapes:
     • Blue boxes for internal modules (CLI, Service, Observer)  
     • Green for external resources (File System, Public Folder)  
     • Orange for third-party libraries/frameworks (Express, JSON5)  

8. Additional Details (per “Give more details” instruction)
   – Show the **test suite** (src/*.test.ts) as a separate module that imports Service and Observer to validate behavior  
   – Include the **CI pipeline** box referencing `.github/workflows`: builds, lints, tests, publishes to npm  
   – Annotate that `package.json` scripts orchestrate `husky` pre-commit hooks and `prettier` formatting  

By following these steps and including all identified modules, interactions, and external dependencies, your system-design diagram will provide an accurate, detail-rich view of **json-server**’s architecture and extension points.
